es: Analizar la tesis, la postura, los recursos retóricos, las salvedades y las implicaciones de un artículo de opinión largo.

teaching.en: The thesis of an opinion article is the central claim its writer defends, and it usually sits in the opening paragraph or returns, sharpened, in the last sentence.
teaching.es: La tesis de un artículo de opinión es la afirmación central que defiende su autor, y suele estar en el párrafo inicial o volver, más afilada, en la última frase.
teaching.explanationEs: No confundas la tesis con lo que el autor solo admite: lo admitido suele ir antes de yet o but.
segments: The thesis of an opinion article is the central claim its writer defends, and
it usually sits in the opening paragraph or returns, sharpened, in the last sentence.
teaching.audioText: The thesis of an opinion article is the central claim its writer defends, and it usually sits in the opening paragraph or returns, sharpened, in the last sentence.

teaching.en: A writer's stance shows in small choices: a phrase such as I would argue or I am not convinced reveals how firmly an opinion is held and how much room is left for doubt.
teaching.es: La postura de quien escribe se nota en pequeñas decisiones: una fórmula como «yo diría que» o «no me convence» revela con qué firmeza se sostiene una opinión y cuánto margen queda para la duda.
teaching.explanationEs: Las fórmulas de postura y los modales (would, may) miden la seguridad del autor.
segments: A writer's stance shows in small choices: a phrase such as I would argue or I am
not convinced reveals how firmly an opinion is held and how much room is left for doubt.
teaching.audioText: A writer's stance shows in small choices: a phrase such as I would argue or I am not convinced reveals how firmly an opinion is held and how much room is left for doubt.

teaching.en: Writers concede a point before they answer it: Much as I understand the worry, the evidence points the other way, and my conclusion stands.
teaching.es: Quien escribe concede un punto antes de responderlo: Aunque entiendo la preocupación, la evidencia apunta en sentido contrario, y mi conclusión se mantiene.
teaching.explanationEs: Conceder no cambia la postura: prepara el terreno para la refutación.
segments: Writers concede a point before they answer it: Much as I understand
the worry, the evidence points the other way, and my conclusion stands.
teaching.audioText: Writers concede a point before they answer it: Much as I understand the worry, the evidence points the other way, and my conclusion stands.

teaching.en: A rhetorical question does not seek information; it invites readers to reach the writer's own answer, as in: What, then, should adults do, if not simply wait?
teaching.es: Una pregunta retórica no busca información; invita al lector a llegar a la respuesta del propio autor, como en: ¿Qué deberían hacer, entonces, los adultos, sino esperar?
teaching.explanationEs: Fíjate en quién responde: si el autor contesta su propia pregunta, su función es guiar al lector.
segments: A rhetorical question does not seek information; it invites readers to reach the writer's
own answer, as in: What, then, should adults do, if not simply wait?
teaching.audioText: A rhetorical question does not seek information; it invites readers to reach the writer's own answer, as in: What, then, should adults do, if not simply wait?

teaching.en: Careful authors add a caveat to every sweeping claim, since a single counterexample could undermine a statement such as all screens damage children.
teaching.es: Los autores cuidadosos añaden una salvedad a cada afirmación demasiado general, porque un solo contraejemplo podría socavar una frase como «todas las pantallas dañan a los niños».
teaching.explanationEs: Una salvedad (of course, that does not mean…) protege la tesis; sin ella, la afirmación es fácil de derribar.
segments: Careful authors add a caveat to every sweeping claim, since a single
counterexample could undermine a statement such as all screens damage children.
teaching.audioText: Careful authors add a caveat to every sweeping claim, since a single counterexample could undermine a statement such as all screens damage children.

teaching.en: The implication of a closing sentence is often the most persuasive part of an essay: children whose minds wander and who never meet boredom may struggle to sit with themselves.
teaching.es: La implicación de una frase final suele ser la parte más persuasiva de un ensayo: los niños cuya mente divaga y que nunca conocen el aburrimiento pueden tener dificultad para estar a solas consigo mismos.
teaching.explanationEs: La implicación es lo que sugiere el texto sin decirlo; pregúntate qué quiere que concluya el lector.
segments: The implication of a closing sentence is often the most persuasive part of an essay:
children whose minds wander and who never meet boredom may struggle to sit with themselves.
teaching.audioText: The implication of a closing sentence is often the most persuasive part of an essay: children whose minds wander and who never meet boredom may struggle to sit with themselves.

prompt.es: Localiza la tesis: ¿qué defiende realmente la autora de este párrafo?

choices.text: Children who are never bored miss a chance to invent.
Long afternoons with nothing to do please almost everyone, whatever their age.
Children should be spared every idle afternoon they dread.

feedback.es: La tesis llega tras «Yet I would argue»; lo anterior es lo que la autora admite sin cambiar de postura.

hint.es: La tesis es la afirmación que defiende, no la que concede al principio.

origin.text: Nobody enjoys a long afternoon with nothing to do, and I do not pretend otherwise. Yet I would argue that children who are never bored miss something important, because boredom is where new ideas begin.

prompt.es: Completa: «Decir que todo daña es una afirmación demasiado general.»

answer.text: sweeping

feedback.es: Un sweeping claim abarca más de lo que puede demostrar; por eso un solo contraejemplo lo derriba.

hint.es: Adjetivo que describe una afirmación que lo abarca todo.

origin.text: To say that every screen harms every child is a ___ claim; one counterexample would be enough to rebut it.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Los niños aburridos suelen inventar juegos y hacer mejores preguntas.»

answer.text: Bored children tend to invent games and ask better questions

feedback.es: Tend to + verbo base expresa una tendencia: el autor matiza en lugar de afirmar que siempre ocurre.

hint.es: El sujeto va primero; tend to lleva el verbo en forma base.

prompt.es: ¿Qué actitud muestra la autora ante la prohibición de los móviles en clase?

choices.text: She welcomes it as the decisive answer to falling results.
She grants it some use but doubts that it tackles the real problem.
She rejects it as damaging and refuses to consider it.
She has no view of her own and only reports what others say.

feedback.es: Concede algo con «may help a little» y no la descarta, pero «treats the symptom» revela que duda de que resuelva el problema de fondo.

origin.text: I am not convinced that banning phones in classrooms will raise results. It may help a little, and I would not rule it out, but a ban treats the symptom and leaves the cause alone.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué efecto busca la pregunta retórica de la autora.

choices.text: To collect suggestions from readers who might disagree with her views.
To admit that she has no practical advice to offer readers.
To lead the reader to a conclusion she has already reached.

feedback.es: La autora contesta su propia pregunta; no pide información, sino que guía al lector hacia su tesis.

origin.audio: What, then, should adults do? Hand over a tablet, and the problem disappears for ten minutes. Leave the silence alone, and something more interesting may grow. She does not wait for an answer. She supplies it, and the reader, having followed her this far, is ready to nod.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada frase del artículo con la función que cumple en el argumento.

pairs: I would argue that boredom is more useful than it seems
Admittedly, some screens have their uses
Is that really too much to ask?
Every screen ruins a child's concentration
Several studies suggest, though none proves, a link

feedback.es: Cada frase desempeña un papel distinto: postura explícita, concesión, pregunta retórica, exceso y reserva.

pairs: I would argue that boredom is more useful than it seems
Admittedly, some screens have their uses
Is that really too much to ask?
Every screen ruins a child's concentration
Several studies suggest, though none proves, a link

prompt.es: ¿Qué da a entender la autora en la última frase, sin decirlo abiertamente?

choices.text: That a quiet hour always produces creative work in every child.
That difficult books and long talks are unsuitable for children.
That children who read little are bound to think poorly.
That constant activity may leave children struggling to concentrate later.

feedback.es: El texto sugiere, sin afirmarlo, que quien nunca se queda a solas tendrá dificultades para concentrarse después; la primera frase descarta lo contrario.

origin.text: It would be wrong to think that every child will turn a quiet hour into a masterpiece. Nevertheless, children who have never learned to sit with themselves may find it hard to sit with anything else, whether a difficult book, a long conversation or their own thoughts.

prompt.es: Escucha el fragmento y elige la actitud de la autora ante los padres preocupados.

choices.text: Understanding enough to soften her main thesis quite a lot.
Understanding, but not ready to move from her main point.
Impatient with them for ignoring the evidence available to everyone.

feedback.es: Comprende la preocupación de los padres, pero el «Yet I would argue» mantiene su tesis: empatía sin cesión.

origin.audio: Some parents will object that boredom is a waste of time, and I understand the worry. Nobody enjoys a long afternoon with nothing to do. Yet I would argue that children who are never bored miss something important. Several studies suggest that bored children tend to invent games, draw and ask better questions, although it would be wrong to claim that every bored child will. The caveat matters: I am not saying that screens are damaging in themselves. What, then, should adults do? Nothing, mostly. Leave the silence alone, and something more interesting may grow there.

prompt.es: Completa: «Un solo contraejemplo bastaría para debilitar todo el argumento.»

answer.text: undermine

feedback.es: Undermine es el verbo habitual para un argumento al que se le quita su base; un sweeping claim es muy vulnerable a él.

origin.text: Suppose the writer claimed that boredom always produces creativity. One counterexample would be enough to ___ the whole argument.

prompt.es: Resume en inglés la postura de la autora: su tesis y la objeción que concede.

answer.text: The writer argues that children should be bored sometimes. Much as she admits that boredom is hard for children, she maintains that it helps them to invent and to reflect.
accepted: The writer argues that children should be bored sometimes. Much as she admits that boredom is hard for children, she maintains that it helps them to invent and to reflect.
The author claims that bored children become more inventive. Although she admits that boredom is dull, she still believes that it helps children to reflect.
The writer maintains that children need some boredom. Much as she accepts that it can be dull, she argues that it helps children to invent more.

feedback.es: Un buen resumen atribuye la tesis con un verbo de postura y deja visible la concesión sin perder la refutación.

origin.text: Artículo «Let Them Be Bored». Defiende que los niños deben aburrirse a veces para inventar y reflexionar. Reconoce que el aburrimiento resulta incómodo. Escribe dos frases con un verbo de postura y una concesión (Much as…).

prompt.es: ¿Con qué propósito escribe la autora este párrafo?

choices.text: To admit that her thesis rests on rather weak evidence.
To answer an expected objection and defend her own thesis more firmly.
To recommend old games as a replacement for screens.
To describe how one child happened to spend an afternoon.

feedback.es: Anticipa la crítica («Critics will say») y la rebate para reforzar su tesis; el niño es solo un ejemplo al servicio del argumento.

origin.text: Critics will say that I am praising doing nothing. I am not. A child left alone with a broken game and a free afternoon is not in pain; she is, in all likelihood, about to have an idea. The alternative, a screen at the first sign of boredom, is only a delay of the moment when the child must face the silence.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Una salvedad limita una afirmación sin abandonarla.»

answer.text: A caveat limits a claim without abandoning it

feedback.es: El verbo limits describe la función de la salvedad; without abandoning it aclara que la afirmación sigue en pie.

prompt.es: Completa: «Cuando se quedan solos, su mente empieza a divagar.»

answer.text: wander

feedback.es: Minds wander es la colocación natural para la mente que divaga sin rumbo fijo.

origin.text: When children are left alone with nothing to do, their minds begin to ___; some of them return with an idea.

title.es: Proyecto de escritura: edición de precisión

es: Editar un borrador con precisión: corregir tiempos, registro, cohesión, conectores y concisión eligiendo el cambio mínimo.

vocabulary.es: releer para detectar erratas y deslices

teaching.en: We edit in layers: meaning first, then cohesion, then wording, and a final proofread for the slips that survive every earlier pass.
teaching.es: Editamos por capas: primero el significado, después la cohesión, luego la redacción y, al final, una relectura para detectar los deslices que sobreviven a todas las pasadas anteriores.
teaching.explanationEs: Revisar todo a la vez hace perder errores; cada capa tiene su propia pregunta.
segments: We edit in layers: meaning first, then cohesion, then wording, and
a final proofread for the slips that survive every earlier pass.
teaching.audioText: We edit in layers: meaning first, then cohesion, then wording, and a final proofread for the slips that survive every earlier pass.

teaching.en: A connector must mirror the real logic of the ideas: in We cut the price; as a result, sales rose, it signals consequence, whereas however would suggest an unexpected contrast.
teaching.es: Un conector debe reflejar la lógica real de las ideas: en Bajamos el precio; como resultado, las ventas subieron, señala consecuencia, mientras que however sugeriría un contraste inesperado.
teaching.explanationEs: Suma (moreover), contrasta (however) o da resultado (as a result): elige según la relación real.
segments: A connector must mirror the real logic of the ideas: in We cut the price;
as a result, sales rose, it signals consequence, whereas however would suggest an unexpected contrast.
teaching.audioText: A connector must mirror the real logic of the ideas: in We cut the price; as a result, sales rose, it signals consequence, whereas however would suggest an unexpected contrast.

teaching.en: A wordy sentence buries its point, so tighten up the draft: In order to finish, we need time becomes To finish, we need time, and the meaning is untouched.
teaching.es: Una frase prolija entierra su idea, así que ajusta el borrador: In order to finish, we need time pasa a To finish, we need time, y el significado queda intacto.
teaching.explanationEs: Si puedes quitar palabras sin perder significado, la frase estaba inflada.
segments: A wordy sentence buries its point, so tighten up the draft: In order to finish,
we need time becomes To finish, we need time, and the meaning is untouched.
teaching.audioText: A wordy sentence buries its point, so tighten up the draft: In order to finish, we need time becomes To finish, we need time, and the meaning is untouched.

teaching.en: Needless repetition makes a sentence wordy: the recently opened shop carries the whole idea, whereas the new, recently opened shop says it twice.
teaching.es: La repetición innecesaria vuelve prolija una frase: the recently opened shop contiene toda la idea, mientras que the new, recently opened shop la dice dos veces.
teaching.explanationEs: New y recently opened cuentan la misma idea: basta con uno de los dos.
segments: Needless repetition makes a sentence wordy: the recently opened shop carries the
whole idea, whereas the new, recently opened shop says it twice.
teaching.audioText: Needless repetition makes a sentence wordy: the recently opened shop carries the whole idea, whereas the new, recently opened shop says it twice.

teaching.en: A lapse in tense is easy to miss, so keep the timeline steady: when the manager arrived, the team had already finished the report and sent it to the council.
teaching.es: Un desliz en el tiempo verbal es fácil de pasar por alto, así que mantén estable la cronología: cuando llegó el jefe, el equipo ya había terminado el informe y se lo había enviado al consejo.
teaching.explanationEs: Lo anterior a otro hecho pasado lleva had + participio; no mezcles tiempos sin motivo.
segments: A lapse in tense is easy to miss, so keep the timeline steady: when the
manager arrived, the team had already finished the report and sent it to the council.
teaching.audioText: A lapse in tense is easy to miss, so keep the timeline steady: when the manager arrived, the team had already finished the report and sent it to the council.

teaching.en: Colloquial phrasing and vague quantities weaken a report, and ambiguity is best removed with exact wording: forty interviews, not a lot of interviews.
teaching.es: La redacción coloquial y las cantidades vagas debilitan un informe, y la ambigüedad se elimina mejor con palabras exactas: cuarenta entrevistas, no muchas entrevistas.
teaching.explanationEs: El registro profesional prefiere cifras y expresiones precisas a fórmulas de conversación.
segments: Colloquial phrasing and vague quantities weaken a report, and ambiguity is best
removed with exact wording: forty interviews, not a lot of interviews.
teaching.audioText: Colloquial phrasing and vague quantities weaken a report, and ambiguity is best removed with exact wording: forty interviews, not a lot of interviews.

prompt.es: Marca 1: elige el conector que respeta la lógica del párrafo.

choices.text: nevertheless
consequently
meanwhile

feedback.es: Revisar el presupuesto es la consecuencia de la mayor asistencia; nevertheless marca contraste y meanwhile sitúa los hechos en paralelo.

hint.es: El segundo hecho es la consecuencia del primero.

origin.text: The library extended its opening hours in March. Attendance rose by a fifth; ___, the budget for cleaning had to be revised.

prompt.es: Completa: «A pesar del retraso, el informe llegó al consejo a tiempo.»

answer.text: Despite

feedback.es: Despite introduce un contraste formal y se une directamente al nombre: despite the delay, sin of.

hint.es: Preposición de contraste que va seguida del nombre sin of.

origin.text: We postponed the survey twice. ___ the delay, the final report still reached the council before the deadline.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Tras revisar el borrador, eliminó toda repetición innecesaria.»

answer.text: Having reviewed the draft, she removed every needless repetition

feedback.es: Having + participio presenta la acción previa y deja un solo sujeto para toda la frase.

hint.es: Empieza con la acción anterior, expresada con having.

prompt.es: Marca 4: ¿qué versión conserva el sentido con menos palabras?

choices.text: On account of the fact that the committee had failed to decide, the vote was put off until next week.
The vote was postponed until next week because the committee was in a position of not having decided.
As the committee had failed to decide, the vote was postponed until next week.
The vote was postponed.

feedback.es: As the committee had failed to decide conserva causa y plazo con menos palabras; la opción más breve pierde información.

origin.text: The minutes of the meeting state: Due to the fact that the committee failed to reach a decision on the matter, the vote was postponed until the following week.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige el principio que ilustra el cambio de la editora.

choices.text: An exact number is far more convincing than a loose impression.
A shorter phrase is always better than a longer one.
A formal connector should replace an informal one.

feedback.es: La editora sustituye una cantidad vaga por una cifra: la precisión hace la frase más creíble, no solo más corta.

origin.audio: In the draft, the writer said that a lot of participants had dropped out. The editor circled the phrase and asked how many. Six of the forty, it turned out. She replaced the phrase with six of the forty participants, and the sentence suddenly carried weight instead of suggestion.

prompt.es: Relaciona cada frase con la relación lógica que establece el conector.

pairs: The roads were closed; consequently, deliveries slipped.
The roads were closed; nevertheless, deliveries arrived.
The roads were closed; moreover, the main bridge was damaged.
Several roads were closed; for instance, the ring road.
The roads were closed, since the river had risen.

feedback.es: Elegir bien el conector depende de la relación real entre las ideas: consecuencia, contraste, suma, ejemplo o causa.

pairs: The roads were closed; consequently, deliveries slipped.
The roads were closed; nevertheless, deliveries arrived.
The roads were closed; moreover, the main bridge was damaged.
Several roads were closed; for instance, the ring road.
The roads were closed, since the river had risen.

prompt.es: Marca 7: corrige el registro y el conector de esta frase del borrador.

answer.text: The figures were rather poor; nevertheless, the board decided to continue with the trial.
accepted: The figures were rather poor; nevertheless, the board decided to continue with the trial.
The figures were somewhat weak; even so, the board decided to go ahead with the trial.
The figures were fairly poor; however, the board decided to carry on with the trial.

feedback.es: El cambio mínimo sustituye pretty bad por una expresión neutra y so por un conector de contraste, porque decidir seguir contradice la decepción.

origin.text: The figures were pretty bad, so the board decided to go ahead with the trial anyway.

evidenceGroups: in spite of this the board

prompt.es: Completa: «Hay que ajustar este párrafo: la mitad de las palabras no aportan nada.»

answer.text: tighten

feedback.es: Tighten up es la colocación habitual para hacer más concisa una sección sin cambiar su contenido.

origin.text: The second paragraph repeats the first in different words. We need to ___ up the whole section, because half of the words add nothing.

prompt.es: Escucha y elige qué sugiere Mia al proponer que Tom lo lea en voz alta.

choices.text: That Tom should rewrite the argument, which she does not find persuasive.
That speaking the text reveals slips the eye skips over.
That the report will persuade the team better if read out loud.

feedback.es: Leer en voz alta es una forma de proofread: el oído detecta cambios de tiempo y repeticiones que la vista pasa por alto.

origin.audio: After reading Tom's draft, Mia did not begin with the errors. She said that the argument was sound and the findings were clear, which made the small problems all the more annoying. Within a single paragraph, the report shifted from past to present, and two paragraphs began with exactly the same sentence. She suggested that he proofread it aloud and then delete every sentence that said the same thing twice. Tom wondered whether she was only being kind, but she insisted that the content was good and the packaging only messy.

prompt.es: Marca 12: ¿a qué se refiere «Such a pattern» en la última frase?

choices.text: To the little time students spend between their classes.
To the difficulty of changing such a habit once formed.
To phone-checking taking the place of conversation.

feedback.es: Such a pattern retoma lo descrito en las dos frases anteriores: mirar el móvil en lugar de conversar.

origin.text: Many students check their phones between classes. This, in turn, shortens the time they spend talking to one another. Such a pattern is hard to change once it sets in.

prompt.es: ¿Qué pretende en realidad la autora de este mensaje sobre el borrador?

choices.text: To praise the draft and leave it exactly as it is.
To suggest that the second section be expanded.
To ask tactfully for a cut she considers necessary.
To cancel the discussion planned for Thursday.

feedback.es: Tras los elogios, «I wonder whether… might be shortened» es una petición cortés pero real de recorte; el resto suaviza el mensaje.

origin.text: Thank you for the draft. The structure is promising, and the examples are well chosen. I wonder, though, whether the second section might be shortened; as it stands, the point arrives rather slowly, and the reader may lose the thread before the first example appears. Perhaps we could discuss it on Thursday, if that suits you.

prompt.es: Ordena: «Cuando llegó el director, ya habíamos terminado el informe.»

answer.text: By the time the director arrived, we had already finished the report
accepted: By the time the director arrived, we had already finished the report
We had already finished the report by the time the director arrived

feedback.es: By the time + pasado simple fija el momento, y lo anterior a él va en pasado perfecto: had already finished.

prompt.es: Marca 11: sustituye el registro coloquial por uno profesional.

answer.text: We made an error in the figures, and the manager was unhappy about it.
accepted: We made an error in the figures, and the manager was unhappy about it.
We made a mistake in the figures, and the director was annoyed about it.
We miscalculated the figures, and the supervisor was dissatisfied about it.

feedback.es: En un informe se evita la expresión de conversación: un sustantivo neutro para el fallo y un adjetivo formal para la reacción mantienen el sentido.

origin.text: We kind of messed up the figures, and the boss was pretty mad about it.

es: Valorar una actuación oral modelo con una rúbrica de cuatro criterios: estructura, precisión, tacto y evidencia.

teaching.en: A rubric sets out the criteria by which we assess a performance, so that a verdict rests on evidence rather than on mood.
teaching.es: Una rúbrica establece los criterios con los que valoramos una actuación, de modo que el veredicto se apoye en pruebas y no en el estado de ánimo.
teaching.explanationEs: Valorar con criterios evita las impresiones vagas del tipo «me gustó» o «me aburrió».
segments: A rubric sets out the criteria by which we assess a performance,
so that a verdict rests on evidence rather than on mood.
teaching.audioText: A rubric sets out the criteria by which we assess a performance, so that a verdict rests on evidence rather than on mood.

teaching.en: The first criterion is structure: a coherent talk opens with a clear purpose, develops two or three reasons in order, and closes by drawing them together.
teaching.es: El primer criterio es la estructura: una charla coherente abre con un propósito claro, desarrolla dos o tres razones en orden y cierra reuniéndolas.
teaching.explanationEs: Se comprueba con las señales de orden: first, second, finally, to sum up.
segments: The first criterion is structure: a coherent talk opens with a clear purpose,
develops two or three reasons in order, and closes by drawing them together.
teaching.audioText: The first criterion is structure: a coherent talk opens with a clear purpose, develops two or three reasons in order, and closes by drawing them together.

teaching.en: The second criterion is accuracy, and any shortcoming here, such as a slip in tense or a misused connector, is judged by how far it blurs the message.
teaching.es: El segundo criterio es la precisión, y cualquier defecto aquí, como un desliz de tiempo o un conector mal usado, se juzga según cuánto difumina el mensaje.
teaching.explanationEs: Un error que no impide entender pesa menos que uno que cambia el sentido.
segments: The second criterion is accuracy, and any shortcoming here, such as a slip in
tense or a misused connector, is judged by how far it blurs the message.
teaching.audioText: The second criterion is accuracy, and any shortcoming here, such as a slip in tense or a misused connector, is judged by how far it blurs the message.

teaching.en: Tact is the third: a skilled speaker concedes a point and softens a request, and does not digress into blame or complaint.
teaching.es: El tacto es el tercero: quien habla con habilidad concede un punto y suaviza una petición, y no se desvía hacia el reproche o la queja.
teaching.explanationEs: Much as…, I was wondering whether… y should it fail son señales de tacto.
segments: Tact is the third: a skilled speaker concedes a point and
softens a request, and does not digress into blame or complaint.
teaching.audioText: Tact is the third: a skilled speaker concedes a point and softens a request, and does not digress into blame or complaint.

teaching.en: The fourth criterion is evidence: a speaker who can cite a survey, a figure or a precise example is harder to ignore than one who says that many people agree.
teaching.es: El cuarto criterio es la evidencia: quien puede citar una encuesta, una cifra o un ejemplo preciso es más difícil de ignorar que quien dice que mucha gente está de acuerdo.
teaching.explanationEs: Una encuesta, una cifra o un ejemplo concreto valen más que «todo el mundo lo piensa».
segments: The fourth criterion is evidence: a speaker who can cite a survey, a figure or
a precise example is harder to ignore than one who says that many people agree.
teaching.audioText: The fourth criterion is evidence: a speaker who can cite a survey, a figure or a precise example is harder to ignore than one who says that many people agree.

teaching.en: A fair verdict names a strength and a weakness, and it quotes the exact words that prove each one.
teaching.es: Un veredicto justo nombra una fortaleza y una debilidad, y cita las palabras exactas que prueban cada una.
teaching.explanationEs: Sin la cita exacta, una valoración es solo una opinión.
segments: A fair verdict names a strength and a weakness, and
it quotes the exact words that prove each one.

origin.audio: I would like to argue that our town needs a night bus. First, a survey of three hundred residents shows that many workers finish after midnight and cannot get home safely. Second, two neighbouring towns introduced a night route last year, and in both cases more people used it than the forecasts had predicted. Much as I appreciate the council's concern about costs, a pilot route would be modest. I was wondering whether we might try it for three months. Should it fail, we will stop. To sum up, a small experiment could spare hundreds of people a dangerous walk home.

origin.audio: I would argue that a four-day week is worth trying, at least in offices. A company I know of tried it for six months, and the number of people off sick fell by a third. Admittedly, some customers may be disappointed to find the doors closed on Fridays. Even so, that cost is small beside the gain in the mood of the staff. Or rather, it is small if the company explains the change in advance. I have noticed that plans of this kind work best when the staff help to design them. Overall, then, I would not insist on the scheme for every firm, but I would certainly let firms experiment.

prompt.es: Responde al caso con postura, ejemplo, concesión y autocorrección (240–300 palabras).

answer.text: I would argue that a city should close its centre to cars, at least on weekends and in the busiest streets. Take my own town: two years ago the main square was full of traffic, and the shopkeepers used to complain that nobody could stop to look at the windows. Once the square became pedestrian, the shops gradually received more visitors, and the noise dropped noticeably. Admittedly, a ban is not free of problems, because older residents may find it harder to reach the centre and some deliveries may arrive late. Much as I accept that risk, I believe it is smaller than it looks, since a free bus and a few parking spaces at the edge can cover most needs. Or rather, it is smaller when the council consults the residents in advance. What I mean is that the plan hinges on preparation, not on enthusiasm. Every choice has a downside, but this one can sway even a sceptical shopkeeper if the trial is honest and limited. On balance, I would propose a six-month experiment, and I would revise the decision calmly once the figures are in.
accepted: I would argue that a city should close its centre to cars, at least on weekends and in the busiest streets. Take my own town: two years ago the main square was full of traffic, and the shopkeepers used to complain that nobody could stop to look at the windows. Once the square became pedestrian, the shops gradually received more visitors, and the noise dropped noticeably. Admittedly, a ban is not free of problems, because older residents may find it harder to reach the centre and some deliveries may arrive late. Much as I accept that risk, I believe it is smaller than it looks, since a free bus and a few parking spaces at the edge can cover most needs. Or rather, it is smaller when the council consults the residents in advance. What I mean is that the plan hinges on preparation, not on enthusiasm. Every choice has a downside, but this one can sway even a sceptical shopkeeper if the trial is honest and limited. On balance, I would propose a six-month experiment, and I would revise the decision calmly once the figures are in.

In my opinion, closing the city centre to cars is worth a serious trial, especially on the streets where people already walk more than they drive. Consider my aunt's bakery: two years ago the customers used to complain about the noise, and the drivers would park in front of the door for an hour. After the street became pedestrian, the bakery sold more, and the pavement was full of families. It is true that a few elderly customers were unhappy at first, because they could not get close by car. Even though that problem is real, I think it is easy to solve with a free bus and a few parking spaces nearby. To put it more precisely, the real difficulty is not the missing road but the lack of preparation. Let me rephrase that: a car-free centre works only when everyone knows how to arrive. Admittedly, not every street can be closed, and a hospital cannot be cut off. Still, many centres could. All in all, the evidence I have seen points to a modest but clear benefit, and I would support a trial.

Admittedly, an app alone may not be enough: it cannot give you a real conversation. Much as I respect the author, I would argue that the claim is too strong. The source seems to rely on a small survey, and its evidence looks anecdotal, so its conclusion may not be reliable. I was wondering whether the author could explain how many students took part. I understand that a short article has little space, and I appreciate the concern about speaking well. Revision: I first wrote that apps are useless for speaking, or rather, I should say that they are useful but not enough. On balance, the best plan is an app plus real conversations, and that is exactly what this course has given me, so I feel confident now.
